findings.description: L402 payment bypass: the agent API route accepts ANY L402 Authorization header as valid without cryptographic verification. It relies entirely on Aperture proxy being configured upstream. If Aperture is absent or misconfigured, a client can send 'Authorization: L402 anything:anything' and gain free access to all gated services (privacy-audit, cycle-signals, compute, data). The comment acknowledges this: 'In production, Aperture handles verification upstream.'
findings.recommendation: Either enforce actual L402 macaroon+preimage verification in this route (using verifyMacaroon + verifyPreimage from the SDK), or add an explicit check that the request is coming from the Aperture proxy (e.g., a shared secret header). Do not trust the L402 header blindly.

findings.description: POST /api/settlement requires no authentication. Any unauthenticated caller can submit a settlement request with arbitrary saleId, saleAmount, referralFeePct, and recipient addresses. While an attacker cannot steal funds directly (a real Lightning payment must be made to trigger ecash minting), they can: (1) create bogus settlement records in the DB, (2) spam/exhaust Cashu mint quote creation, (3) enumerate valid saleIds via idempotency responses, and (4) trigger Fedimint invite lookups.
findings.recommendation: Require authentication for POST /api/settlement. Use requireAuth(request) or verify a shared secret header (e.g., X-Marketplace-Secret) for server-to-server calls from Teneo Marketplace. Validate that the caller's pubkey is authorized to initiate settlements.

findings.description: Both lib/auth-middleware.ts and middleware.ts fall back to the hardcoded string 'dev-secret-change-in-production' if NEXTAUTH_SECRET and AUTH_SECRET are not set. If a production deployment is misconfigured and these env vars are missing, all session tokens will be signed with this known-public key. An attacker who knows this default (it's in the public source code) can forge valid session tokens for any Nostr pubkey.
findings.recommendation: Remove the hardcoded fallback. Throw a hard error at startup if NEXTAUTH_SECRET is not set in production (env-check.ts already validates this, but the fallback in auth-middleware.ts undermines it). validateRequiredEnv() must be called at startup and must halt the server if critical vars are missing.

findings.description: When MACAROON_ROOT_KEY is not configured, the L402 route logs a FATAL error but continues to serve requests. Lines 321-326 show it falls back to issuing unsigned base64 macaroons. This makes every L402 token forgeable: an attacker can craft any macaroon payload, base64-encode it, and reuse it indefinitely to access gated resources. The verifyMacaroon function returns null when MACAROON_ROOT_KEY is absent (line 87), causing the verification check (line 219-227) to be skipped entirely.
findings.recommendation: Return a 503 Service Unavailable response if MACAROON_ROOT_KEY is not set in production. Never issue unsigned macaroons in production. The fallback should only be active in explicit development mode (NODE_ENV === 'development').

findings.description: GET /api/community, GET /api/merchants, and GET /api/transactions all lack authentication. These endpoints return potentially sensitive data: community deployment configs (including network settings, agent config, federation invite structure), merchant payment addresses (Cashu, Lightning), and full transaction history. An unauthenticated attacker can enumerate all communities, merchants, and financial transactions without any credentials.
findings.recommendation: Add requireAuth() to all three GET endpoints, or at minimum scope them: require auth for full data, return only public fields for unauthenticated requests. At minimum, the transaction history endpoint must require auth as it contains financial records.

findings.description: GET /api/settlement/:id and GET /api/settlement?saleId=... require no authentication and return full settlement details including recipient Cashu address, Fedimint invite codes, Lightning invoices, and mint URLs. The 'notes' field leaks the full internal JSON blob. An attacker can probe for valid settlement IDs (which are DB UUIDs or in-memory IDs) and retrieve recipient payment details.
findings.recommendation: Add authentication to GET /api/settlement endpoints. The full notes payload should not be returned to unauthenticated callers. Strip sensitive fields like recipientFedimintInvite from public responses.

findings.description: Agent, L402, and cycle API routes have CORS set to wildcard '*'. While these are payment-gated endpoints, the wildcard CORS combined with the L402 bypass vulnerability (finding #1) means any web page on the internet can make requests to these endpoints. Additionally, payment route CORS falls back to '*' for server-to-server calls without Origin header (line 197-198), which may be too permissive.
findings.recommendation: Restrict CORS to specific origins for agent/L402 routes if possible. At minimum, document clearly that '*' is intentional for agent commerce scenarios. For the server-to-server case, consider using a shared secret header instead of relying on CORS '*' fallback.

findings.description: The Content-Security-Policy includes both 'unsafe-eval' and 'unsafe-inline' for script-src. While 'unsafe-eval' is required for WASM (noted in comment), the combination of both directives effectively eliminates XSS protection from the CSP. Any injected script tag or eval-based code can execute. The XSS filter in validateCommunityName (lib/validation.ts line 22) only blocks '<script' patterns and would not prevent other XSS vectors.
findings.recommendation: Use nonce-based CSP to allow specific inline scripts without 'unsafe-inline'. For WASM, 'unsafe-eval' alone suffices — nonces can handle the inline scripts. Alternatively use a hash-based approach. Also harden validateCommunityName to use a stricter allowlist approach rather than a denylist regex.

findings.description: Both rate limiters (lib/rate-limiter.ts and lib/rate-limit.ts) use in-process Maps for state. In a multi-instance or serverless deployment (e.g., multiple Next.js workers, Vercel serverless functions), each instance has its own rate limit state. An attacker can exceed rate limits by distributing requests across server instances. This makes rate limiting ineffective at scale.
findings.recommendation: Use a shared, persistent rate limit store for production deployments (e.g., Redis, Upstash, or a database counter). The current implementation is acceptable only for single-instance deployments.

findings.description: The SKIP_PAYMENT_VERIFY bypass in the agent route does NOT check NODE_ENV === 'production'. If this env var is accidentally set on a production server, all payment checks are bypassed silently (only a console.warn is emitted). The l402 route does check for production (line 267-270) and ignores the flag, but the agent route does not.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit check: if SKIP_PAYMENT_VERIFY is set AND NODE_ENV === 'production', log a FATAL error and do NOT bypass payment — return a 500 error or ignore the flag. The bypass should only work in development mode.

findings.description: Payment challenges are stored in an in-process Map. After any server restart, all pending challenges are lost. Users who paid a Lightning invoice but haven't completed verification will have their payment lost (the preimage won't match any stored challenge). This is also a DoS vector: if an attacker can trigger server restarts, they can invalidate all pending payments.
findings.recommendation: Persist payment challenges to the database (or Redis) so they survive server restarts. At minimum, implement a recovery mechanism so users can re-submit their preimage if the challenge was lost.

findings.code_snippet:
} catch (error: any) {
  console.error('[ArxMint] GET /api/cycle error:', error.message, error.stack);
findings.description: The cycle API catch block uses 'catch(error: any)' and logs error.stack to the server console. While stack traces are not sent to the client (the response only returns 'Internal server error'), stack traces in logs can reveal file paths, framework internals, and application structure to operators. More importantly, using 'any' type bypasses TypeScript's error-handling guarantees.
findings.recommendation: Change 'catch (error: any)' to 'catch (error: unknown)' for consistency with the rest of the codebase. Use structured logging (logger.error) instead of console.error for stack traces to ensure proper log redaction.

findings.description: Session revocation is not implemented. HMAC-signed tokens cannot be individually invalidated without a blocklist. Once issued, a session token remains valid for 7 days even after logout. If a user's session token is compromised (e.g., via XSS), there is no way to revoke it immediately. Logout only clears the client-side cookie — the token itself remains valid.
findings.recommendation: Implement a server-side blocklist using the database (a revoked_tokens table with the token's HMAC signature and expiry). The blocklist can be pruned of expired tokens automatically. This is especially important for a financial application.

findings.description: GET /api/payment/status/:id requires no authentication and returns the full PaymentChallenge object including Lightning invoice and macaroon data. An attacker who guesses or obtains a challenge ID can see the associated invoice. Challenge IDs are either the macaroon itself (for L402) or a timestamp+random string (for Cashu), making L402 challenge IDs particularly sensitive since they are also used as verification keys.
findings.recommendation: Require authentication for the payment status endpoint, or return only minimal information (status, expiresAt) without exposing the full challenge object including macaroon and invoice to unauthenticated callers.

findings.code_snippet:
if (/<script/i.test(trimmed))
  throw new ValidationError('name', 'Invalid characters in name');
findings.description: The XSS check in validateCommunityName only blocks the ',
findings.recommendation: If server-side HTML rendering is introduced, use a proper HTML sanitization library (e.g., DOMPurify on the client). For API contexts, consider allowing all characters and relying on output encoding. If a denylist is required, use a comprehensive one or switch to an allowlist approach (letters, numbers, spaces, basic punctuation only).

findings.description: next.config.ts sets typescript.ignoreBuildErrors: true and eslint.ignoreDuringBuilds: true. While this is a build configuration rather than a runtime vulnerability, silencing TypeScript errors can hide type-related security issues (e.g., unvalidated user input being passed as a typed parameter). Security-relevant type errors may be silently ignored during CI/CD builds.
findings.recommendation: Remove ignoreBuildErrors: true and ignoreDuringBuilds: true. Fix any remaining type errors properly. For a financial application, type safety is a security property.

context.summary: ArxMint has a solid security foundation: HMAC-signed sessions with timing-safe comparisons, NIP-98 event freshness and URL binding, httpOnly/sameSite:strict cookies, Prisma parameterized queries (no SQL injection), structured error responses that hide stack traces, rate limiting at middleware and route levels, and comprehensive security headers (HSTS, CSP, X-Frame-Options, etc.). However, four HIGH severity findings require attention before production deployment. Most critical: the L402 agent route trusts any L402 header without cryptographic verification (relying on Aperture being present), and the settlement endpoint accepts unauthenticated POST requests. The hardcoded fallback session secret and unsigned-macaroon fallback when MACAROON_ROOT_KEY is absent are configuration risks that could be catastrophic if env vars are misconfigured. Medium findings center on unauthenticated read access to financial data (communities, merchants, transactions), in-memory state that doesn't survive restarts, and wildcard CORS on payment-gated routes. No SQL injection, command injection, or hardcoded production credentials were found in committed code.
